title: Energy Bands in Solids
short_intro: Energy bands arise from the splitting of discrete atomic energy levels into continuous bands of allowed energies due to the strong interatomic interactions in a crystal lattice. They provide the fundamental theoretical framework for classifying solids into conductors, semiconductors, and insulators.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative classification of solids (conductors, semiconductors, insulators) using valence and conduction bands, forbidden energy gaps, and basic effect of temperature.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Kronig-Penney model (periodic potential), effective mass of electrons, Bloch's theorem, Fermi-Dirac distribution function, and intrinsic/extrinsic carrier concentration calculations.

prerequisites: Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom and atomic energy levels
Pauli's exclusion principle and electron spin
Wave-particle duality and de Broglie wavelength

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Energy Bands
bullets: When isolated atoms are brought together to form a crystal, outer shell electrons interact strongly with neighboring atomic potentials.
According to Pauli's exclusion principle, identical electrons cannot occupy the same quantum state, causing degenerate energy levels to split.
For N atoms, each atomic level splits into N closely spaced energy levels forming a continuous energy band.

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Solids
bullets: Insulators possess a large forbidden energy gap (E<sub>g</sub> > 3 eV) with a completely filled valence band and empty conduction band.
Semiconductors have a narrow forbidden gap (E<sub>g</sub> &approx; 1 eV), allowing thermal excitation of electrons from the valence to the conduction band.
Conductors feature overlapping valence and conduction bands or a half-filled band, ensuring free movement of charge carriers under an electric field.

concept_notes.heading: Bloch Theorem and Periodic Potential
bullets: The potential energy V(x) experienced by an electron in a crystal lattice is periodic with the lattice constant a, such that V(x) = V(x + a).
Solutions to the Schrödinger equation for a periodic potential are modulated plane waves known as Bloch functions: ψ<sub>k</sub>(x) = u<sub>k</sub>(x)exp(i k x).
The periodic potential leads to the formation of allowed energy bands separated by forbidden energy gaps in the E-k dispersion relation.

concept_notes.heading: Effective Mass of Electrons
bullets: Inside a crystal lattice, an electron responds to external electric fields as if it possesses an effective mass m* rather than its rest mass m<sub>0</sub>.
The effective mass is defined by the curvature of the E-k band: m* = ℏ<sup>2</sup> / (d<sup>2</sup>E / dk<sup>2</sup>).
Near the bottom of an energy band, m* is positive, whereas near the top of a band, the curvature is negative, yielding a negative effective mass interpreted as holes.

derivations.title: Kronig-Penney Model Energy Dispersion Relation
derivations.conditions: 1D rectangular periodic potential well of height V<sub>0</sub> and width b, barrier width a-b.
steps: Apply Bloch's theorem to the Schrödinger equation in regions of zero potential and square-well potential.
Match the wavefunctions and their first derivatives at the boundary x = b.
Apply boundary conditions and simplify using the approximation of a rectangular delta-function potential where V<sub>0</sub> → ∞ and b → 0 keeping P = (m V<sub>0</sub> b a) / ℏ<sup>2</sup> constant.
Obtain the transcendental equation: (P / α a) sin(α a) + cos(α a) = cos(k a), where α<sup>2</sup> = 2mE / ℏ<sup>2</sup>.
derivations.result: The transcendental equation constrains allowed values of αa such that the left-hand side must lie strictly between -1 and +1, yielding allowed energy bands and forbidden gaps.

derivations.title: Density of States in a 3D Energy Band
derivations.conditions: Free electron approximation in a 3D box of volume V.
steps: Write the energy of an electron as E = (ℏ<sup>2</sup> k<sup>2</sup>) / (2m*), where k<sup>2</sup> = k<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> + k<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> + k<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup>.
Calculate the number of allowed k-states in a spherical shell of radius k and thickness dk in k-space as N(k) dk = 2 * (4 π k<sup>2</sup> dk) / (8 π<sup>3</sup> / V).
Differentiate the energy relation to find dk/dE and substitute it into the state density expression N(E)dE = N(k)dk.

graphs_and_experiments.title: E vs k Dispersion Relation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of energy E versus wave vector k showing reduced zone scheme with Brillouin zones, separated by forbidden energy gaps.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Discontinuities in the E-k curve occur at k = ± nπ/a, which correspond to Bragg reflection planes defining the boundaries of forbidden energy bands.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested for identifying zone boundaries, forbidden gaps, and regions of positive/negative effective mass.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fermi-Dirac Distribution Function vs Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of f(E) versus E for T = 0 K (step function) and T > 0 K (smoothly sloping curve passing through f(E<sub>F</sub>) = 0.5).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At T = 0 K, all states below E<sub>F</sub> are completely filled and those above are empty. As temperature rises, thermal excitation smears the occupation probability around E<sub>F</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining thermal generation of carriers and temperature dependence of semiconductor Fermi levels.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hall Effect Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A semiconductor slab carrying current I<sub>x</sub> placed in a transverse magnetic field B<sub>z</sub>, generating a transverse Hall voltage V<sub>H</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The sign of the Hall coefficient R<sub>H</sub> confirms whether the majority charge carriers are electrons (negative) or holes (positive), validating band theory predictions.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to determine carrier concentration, sign of charge carriers, and mobility in solids.

solved_numericals.question: A solid has a forbidden energy gap of 1.2 eV. Calculate the maximum wavelength of a photon that can excite an electron from the valence band to the conduction band.
solution_steps: Identify given values: E_g = 1.2 eV = 1.2 * 1.6 * 10^-19 J.
Use the photon energy relation: E_g = \frac{hc}{\lambda}.
Substitute constants h = 6.63 * 10^-34 J s and c = 3 * 10^8 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: The E-k relationship for electrons in a one-dimensional crystal band is given by E(k) = E_0 - 2A \cos(a k), where A and a are constants. Find the expression for the effective mass m* of the electron at the bottom of the band (k = 0).
solution_steps: State the effective mass formula: m* = \hbar^{2} / (d^{2}E / dk^{2}).
Differentiate E(k) with respect to k once: \frac{dE}{dk} = 2Aa \sin(ak).
Evaluate at the bottom of the band where k = 0: \left.\frac{d^{2}E}{dk^{2}}\right|_{k=0} = 2Aa^{2}.
Substitute into the effective mass expression: m* = \hbar^{2} / (2Aa^{2}).

solved_numericals.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor with a band gap of 0.7 eV, calculate the probability of an energy state being occupied by an electron at 0.3 eV above the Fermi level at a temperature of 300 K. (Take k_B = 8.62 * 10^-5 eV/K)
solution_steps: Identify given values: E - E_F = 0.3 eV, T = 300 K, k_B = 8.62 * 10^-5 eV/K.
Write down the Fermi-Dirac distribution function: f(E) = 1 / [exp((E - E_F) / (k_B T)) + 1].
Calculate the exponent term: (E - E_F) / (k_B T) = 0.3 / (8.62 \times 10^{-5} \times 300) = 0.3 / 0.02586 = 11.60.

assumptions_and_limitations: The one-electron approximation assumes each electron moves in an average effective potential created by the ionic cores and all other electrons.

The adiabatic (Born-Oppenheimer) approximation assumes atomic nuclei are stationary compared to rapidly moving electrons, which fails at high temperatures where lattice vibrations (phonons) strongly couple with electrons.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electrons in a completely filled valence band can contribute to electrical conduction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Completely filled valence bands do not conduct electricity.
common_misconceptions.why: Under an applied electric field, every electron moving in one direction has a corresponding electron moving in the opposite direction, resulting in zero net current.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The effective mass of an electron in a crystal is always positive and equal to its rest mass.
common_misconceptions.correct: The effective mass can be negative or different in magnitude from the rest mass.
common_misconceptions.why: Effective mass depends on the local curvature of the E-k dispersion curve, which is dictated by the periodic crystal potential.

quick_revision: Band gaps arise from Bragg reflections of electron waves at the Brillouin zone boundaries in periodic crystal potentials.
